clue.text: Fine Italian hand perhaps employed by the BBC?

definitions.text: Fine Italian hand perhaps employed by the BBC?

parts.words: Fine Italian hand perhaps employed by the BBC?
parts.note: an 'Italian hand' is a style of elegant handwriting, so one who writes it well might be so called; really it is someone who writes scripts for broadcasters

explanation.surface: Somebody with beautiful Italian penmanship lands a job at the BBC.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads first as calligraphy; the second half shifts to the person who writes broadcast scripts.
explanation.definitionFit: Broadcasters employ people who compose the words spoken in their programmes, and 'script' also means handwriting.

clue.text: Defamation of decapitated Cypriot, for instance

indicators.note: beheaded, so the first letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: a Cypriot lives on an island, so is an example of an islander

explanation.surface: A headless body from Cyprus is the subject of a libel case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'decapitated' removes the head (first letter) of ISLANDER, a Cypriot being an example of an island dweller.
explanation.definitionFit: Slander is spoken defamation, false statements that damage a reputation.

clue.text: Coloured girl in Cornwall

definitions.note: stands for a place located in that county

parts.note: red is a colour
Ruth is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl with red colouring lives in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: Redruth is a town in Cornwall, the county at England's south-western tip; the definition is 'in Cornwall', i.e. a place there.
explanation.definitionFit: Redruth is an old mining town in west Cornwall.

clue.text: Separate watch is not fully employed

parts.note: to part is to separate
a watch is a timepiece, a timer

explanation.surface: A broken watch isn't keeping full time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'watch' is a noun giving TIMER, not the verb to look.
explanation.definitionFit: A person working only some of the standard hours has a job that is less than full-time.

clue.text: Wielded by fairy godmothers in two quarters

definitions.meaning: a fairy godmother waves a magic stick
..., two compass points, written as west and south joined by the word 'and'

explanation.surface: Fairy godmothers operate in two different districts.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass points W and S are 'quarters'; written as W AND S they spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Magic sticks are what fairy godmothers wave, and W and S spells the same letters.

clue.text: Put in danger of empire suffering a loss

indicators.note: undergoing, so the word is about to lose something
a loss means a letter is taken away from the word

parts.note: imperial means relating to an empire

explanation.surface: An empire is endangered by a defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of empire' gives IMPERIAL; 'suffering a loss' removes its A.
explanation.definitionFit: To imperil is to endanger or put at risk.

clue.text: A gentle way of becoming graceful

indicators.note: says the letters of the phrase are made into another arrangement

explanation.surface: Being gentle is one route to grace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'way of becoming' signals an anagram of A GENTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegant means stylish and refined, synonymous with graceful.

clue.text: Name part impersonated by another in farce

definitions.text: Name part impersonated by another in farce

parts.words: Name part impersonated by another in farce
parts.note: refers to a Victorian farce whose title role, a rich relative from Brazil, is impersonated by an undergraduate in drag

explanation.surface: An instruction to identify a role played by an impostor in a comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Brandon Thomas's 1892 farce has Lord Fancourt Babberley disguise himself as his friend's aunt from Brazil.
explanation.definitionFit: In this famous English farce, the title character is played by a young man in disguise.

clue.text: Mother Hubbard evidently wasn't one

parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Old Mother Hubbard found her cupboard bare, so she had clearly not been stockpiling food

explanation.surface: A remark about the nursery-rhyme old woman with the empty cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Mother Hubbard is a nursery-rhyme character whose cupboard was bare when she went to fetch her dog a bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who stockpiles supplies would never have an empty cupboard.

clue.text: Tom Pinch's children?

parts.note: to pinch is to nip, so the offspring of a man named Pinch might jokingly be called by a word that also means small children

explanation.surface: A question about the family of Tom Pinch, a character in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Pinch is a Dickens character; read his surname as the verb 'pinch' = nip, and those who nip are also slang for little children.
explanation.definitionFit: Small children are informally called nippers, and nippers are also things that pinch.

clue.text: He has a moving role in 24

definitions.text: He has a moving role in 24

parts.words: He has a moving role in 24
parts.note: a 'moving role' sounds like an emotional part in a play, but this stagehand's job is literally moving scenery

explanation.surface: An actor has a touching part in a stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 across is THEATRE; the 'moving role' is shifting sets, not touching an audience.
explanation.definitionFit: A stagehand who changes the sets between scenes in a playhouse.

clue.text: Our debt could be to the military, for defence

indicators.note: says the letters of the preceding words might be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Money we owe to the armed forces is spent on national defence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges OUR DEBT; 'to the military' sets the defence in an army context.
explanation.definitionFit: A redoubt is a small enclosed fortification built to defend a position.

clue.text: Aquatic champion, on top, naturally

parts.note: surf is the breaking sea, the watery element
an ace is an expert or champion

explanation.surface: A swimming champion naturally finishes in first place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aquatic' gives SURF and 'champion' ACE; 'naturally' is a link meaning 'of course'.
explanation.definitionFit: Surface as an adjective describes what lies at the uppermost layer, outward rather than deep.

clue.text: On the face of it, aren't we all?

definitions.text: On the face of it, aren't we all?

parts.words: On the face of it, aren't we all?
parts.note: 'on the face of it' usually means apparently, but here it means literally living on the surface of our planet

explanation.surface: A rhetorical question asking whether, apparently, everyone is the same.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'on the face of it' is taken literally: all of us live on the face of the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Our planet's surface is where every human lives.

clue.text: This hanger-on is above kissing!

parts.note: a hanger-on is usually a sycophant, but here it is a plant hung up at Christmas under which people kiss, and is also a parasite

explanation.surface: Someone sniffs that a toady considers themselves too grand for kissing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Above kissing' sounds like snobbery, but it is literal: the sprig hangs above couples who kiss beneath it. The plant is also a parasite, a true hanger-on.
explanation.definitionFit: The parasitic Christmas sprig hung from ceilings is the traditional place under which couples kiss.

clue.text: A sight, one of two for myopic viewers?

definitions.text: one of two for myopic viewers
definitions.meaning: the singular of the pair of lenses worn by the short-sighted

explanation.surface: A remark about eye-glasses for short-sighted people.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectacle is an impressive display, and glasses are called spectacles, a pair of lenses.

clue.text: Proverbially not to be made of pigskin

definitions.text: Proverbially not to be made of pigskin

parts.words: Proverbially not to be made of pigskin
parts.note: alludes to the proverb that you cannot make a fine luxury item out of a sow's ear

explanation.surface: A remark that, according to the proverb, something cannot be made from pig hide.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'you can't make a silk purse out of a sow's ear'; 'pigskin' stands in for the sow's ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says this fine bag cannot be fashioned from a sow's ear, which is pigskin.

clue.text: Upholder of Holy Writ

parts.note: 'upholder' suggests a defender of scripture, but here it is the stand that physically holds up the Bible in church

explanation.surface: A description of a defender of the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upholder' is taken literally: a reading stand holding the Bible up.
explanation.definitionFit: A church's reading stand supports the Bible for the reader.

clue.text: You'll love me for giving you this

definitions.text: You'll love me for giving you this

parts.words: You'll love me for giving you this
parts.note: sounds like a gift-giver's boast, but the gift is a magic potion making the drinker fall in love with the giver

explanation.surface: A gift-giver confident that the present will win affection.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'love' is literal: this drink is a love potion.
explanation.definitionFit: A philtre is a magic drink meant to arouse love.

clue.text: One sort of bull has flag with his initial on

parts.note: a flag is a kind of iris, the plant

indicators.note: the initial of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A bull in a field wears a flag bearing the owner's initial.
explanation.walkthrough: An Irish bull is a ludicrous self-contradictory statement, not an animal; 'flag' is the plant, not a banner.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irish bull is a statement containing a comic contradiction, a recognised kind of verbal blunder.

clue.text: More ski trouble? How irritating !

indicators.note: trouble, as disorder, says the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A skier, plagued by further problems with equipment, sighs in irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' signals an anagram of MORE SKI.
explanation.definitionFit: Irksome means annoying or tiresome.

clue.text: If music be the food of love, are these the teeth?

definitions.text: If music be the food of love, are these the teeth?

parts.words: If music be the food of love, are these the teeth?
parts.note: Twelfth Night's opening line makes music food; the piano keys, once made of tusk, are slang for both keys and teeth

explanation.surface: A whimsical extension of Shakespeare's line about music feeding love.
explanation.walkthrough: Orsino's line from Twelfth Night is extended: if music is food, the piano keys would be its teeth. The slang word covers both keys and teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Piano keys and teeth are both slangily called by the name of elephant tusk material.

clue.text: Some young 'uns can be rich 'uns!

indicators.note: says the letters of the following words may be turned into another arrangement

explanation.surface: A cheery remark that some youngsters may turn out wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' signals an anagram of RICH 'UNS (the apostrophe is not a letter).
explanation.definitionFit: Urchins are mischievous young children, often ragged street kids.

clue.text: This stake is no use as a broomstick

definitions.text: This stake is no use as a broomstick

parts.words: This stake is no use as a broomstick
parts.note: the word combines with 'stake' to form a lottery-style bet, and is also what a broom does

explanation.surface: A remark that a wooden stake makes a poor broom handle.
explanation.walkthrough: A sweepstake is a betting pool; 'stake' is the bet, not a post.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweepstake is a gamble in which the winner takes all the stakes; the first half also means to brush the floor.

clue.text: Naturists need no runway to do this

definitions.text: Naturists need no runway to do this

parts.words: Naturists need no runway to do this
parts.note: an aircraft needs a runway to leave the ground, but nudists remove clothes without one

explanation.surface: A joke that nudists can get airborne without an airstrip.
explanation.walkthrough: The aviation sense of leaving the ground is replaced by the phrasal verb for removing clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Removing one's clothes is phrased with the same words as an aircraft leaving the ground.

clue.text: Globe, containing "all the world"

parts.note: the Globe was Shakespeare's playhouse, and in As You Like It 'all the world's a stage'

explanation.surface: A globe holds the whole world on its surface.
explanation.walkthrough: The Globe is Shakespeare's London playhouse; 'All the world's a stage' is from As You Like It, so a stage building contains all the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Globe was a playhouse, and his line equates the world with a stage.

clue.text: Old footwear a little too long for a composer

definitions.text: Old footwear a little too long for a composer

parts.words: Old footwear a little too long for a composer
parts.note: an old platform shoe whose name is a Polish pianist-composer's surname with one letter too many tacked on the end

explanation.surface: Antique shoes that don't quite fit a composer's feet.
explanation.walkthrough: The old shoe's name is CHOPIN plus E: 'a little too long' for the composer's name by one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A chopine was a tall platform shoe worn in Renaissance Europe.

clue.text: They are evidently not tongue-tied

parts.note: tongue-tied means lost for words; these people are fluent in more than one tongue, meaning language

explanation.surface: A remark about some articulate, talkative people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tongue' here means a language: these people convert speech between languages.
explanation.definitionFit: Translators of speech must be fluent in several languages.
